item.title: Mainland expresses thanks to various sectors in Taiwan for concern over mudslide disaster
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-02
Mainland expresses thanks to various sectors in Taiwan for concern over mudslide disaster Source: XinhuaUpdated: 2026-09-02
BEIJING, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- A Chinese mainland spokesperson on Wednesday expressed appreciation to people from various sectors in Taiwan for their concern after a devastating mudslide struck Gyirong border Port in southwest Xizang Autonomous Region. "No one from Taiwan was reported missing, hurt or dead from the disaster," said Zhang Han, spokesperson for the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office. "We will keep following the situation and provide necessary assistance in a timely manner to Taiwan compatriots in the stricken area," she said. An ice-rock avalanche in Nepal triggered a deadly mudslide that hit Gyirong Port on the Chinese side on Aug. 26. According to the latest update of the Xizang regional government, the disaster has claimed 16 lives and left 546 others missing at the border port. In response to a media question, Zhang expressed concern over the disruption to normal life and work caused by continuous heavy rain in southern Taiwan and willingness to provide help. item.title: Mainland denounces Taiwan authorities' move to increase defense spending
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-02
Mainland denounces Taiwan authorities' move to increase defense spending Source: XinhuaUpdated: 2026-09-02
BEIJING, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- A Chinese mainland spokesperson on Wednesday criticized the decision of Taiwan authorities led by Lai Ching-te to raise the island's defense budget in 2027, saying it would only bring grave disaster to the people in Taiwan. Zhang Han, spokesperson for the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office, made the remarks in response to a question about the island's defense budget of more than 1 trillion New Taiwan dollars (about 31 billion U.S. dollars) for 2027, which Taiwan authorities led by Lai Ching-te said was aimed at strengthening its defense capabilities and demonstrating its resolve to defend itself. Zhang said Taiwan authorities led by Lai Ching-te have stubbornly adhered to their separatist stance of seeking "Taiwan independence," disregarding the mainstream public opinion on the island that calls for "peace, development, cross-Strait exchanges and cooperation." They have instead stoked confrontation across the Taiwan Strait and squandered public funds in pursuit of their independence agenda, Zhang said, adding that such efforts are "simply beyond their capabilities" and will only have serious consequences for the people of Taiwan. "We are unwavering in our resolve and formidable in our ability to safeguard national sovereignty and territorial integrity, and will never leave any room for separatist activities seeking 'Taiwan independence' in any form," Zhang noted. She called on people in Taiwan to recognize the dangers of "Taiwan independence" separatism, firmly oppose such activities, and safeguard the common home of the Chinese nation. Taiwan's executive authorities approved the island's 2027 general budget on Aug. 20, with defense spending rising sharply to over 1 trillion New Taiwan dollars for the first time. The defense budget accounts for roughly 29 percent of total government expenditure, meaning that about 29 out of every 100 New Taiwan dollars in government spending would go toward defense. item.title: Taipei Zoo celebrates 22nd birthday of giant panda from mainland
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-31
Taipei Zoo celebrates 22nd birthday of giant panda from mainland Source: XinhuaUpdated: 2026-08-31
TAIPEI -- Visitors gathered at Taipei Zoo on Sunday to celebrate the 22nd birthday of Yuan Yuan, the female giant panda gifted by the Chinese mainland to Taiwan. The zoo prepared a small train-themed "cake," sugarcane "candles" shaped to make the number "22," and bite-sized pieces of carrots and grapes as her birthday meal. The meal was tailored to Yuan Yuan's dietary preferences, with careful attention to ingredient combinations and behavioral enrichment to encourage her to forage, grab and chew her food independently, according to the zoo. Yuan Yuan seemed to like the "candles" most. Large numbers of visitors came to the zoo to wish Yuan Yuan a happy birthday, and the celebration was also shared online. At 22, Yuan Yuan is considered elderly for a giant panda. During her annual health checkup last November, the zoo found that the functions of her major organs, including her heart and digestive system, remained generally stable, but signs of aging had emerged in her eyes, kidneys and spine. The zoo has since placed her under enhanced senior care and closer observation, incorporating age-related changes into her routine health-monitoring records. Yuan Yuan and her male companion Tuan Tuan, both four years old at the time, arrived in Taipei as goodwill gifts from the mainland in 2008. Since then, the zoo has worked closely with mainland conservation institutions on breeding, physiology and veterinary care, with experts and staff making continuous visits and exchanging technical expertise. The pair had two female offspring, Yuan Zai and Yuan Bao, born in 2013 and 2020, respectively. Tuan Tuan died of illness in November 2022 at the age of 18. Related Stories

item.title: Economic Watch: Structural imbalances persist amid Taiwan's economic growth
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-31
Economic Watch: Structural imbalances persist amid Taiwan's economic growth Source: XinhuaUpdated: 2026-08-31
TAIPEI, Aug. 31 (Xinhua) -- Recent economic data from Taiwan show a widening gap between a booming high-tech manufacturing sector and traditional industries that continue to struggle. Industry groups and economists on the island say the persistent imbalances call for a more balanced allocation of industrial resources, so that the rapid expansion of one sector does not come at the expense of others. That concern was highlighted in a 2026 report released last week by the Taiwan Federation of Industries, following a survey of 161 industry associations affiliated with the federation. The report said Taiwan authorities have for years placed disproportionate policy emphasis on semiconductors and other high-tech industries. The policy bias has helped drive the tech sector's strong growth, with exports reaching record highs and wealth generated by the tech boom pushing up asset and housing prices. Meanwhile, workers in traditional manufacturing have faced stagnant wages and rising living costs. The contrast, the report said, has created a veneer of prosperity in the statistics while exposing deeper structural strains in Taiwan's economy. The latest trade and industrial production data show how the structural imbalances are playing out across industries. Export orders for information and communications technology products jumped 89.5 percent in July from a year earlier, while orders for electronic products also posted strong growth, according to figures released by Taiwan's economic authorities. By contrast, several traditional industries saw weak demand in July. Orders for chemicals and plastic and rubber products edged up only slightly year on year, while those for optical products fell by more than 10 percent. The divergence was even more striking in industrial production. In July, Taiwan's output of computers, electronics and optical products surged 95.62 percent from a year earlier. Yet production in several traditional industries, including chemicals, fertilizers and automobiles, declined. Taiwan's labor market also shows a structural mismatch. Taiwan's statistics authorities reported that the unemployment rate among people aged 15 to 24 stood at 11.71 percent in July, well above the overall unemployment rate. At the same time, businesses continue to report difficulty finding workers. Some 76.6 percent of the industry associations surveyed for the 2026 report identified labor shortages as their biggest challenge, making it the top concern for the third consecutive year. The coexistence of relatively high youth unemployment and widespread labor shortages points to a mismatch between the jobs being created and the skills available to fill them, according to Tsai Ming-fang, an economics professor at Tamkang University. As technology-driven sectors demand increasingly specialized skills, some job seekers face higher barriers to entering those industries, Tsai said. The disconnect is particularly striking against the backdrop of Taiwan's strong economic growth. Taiwan's statistics agency reported in late July that the island's gross domestic product expanded 12.92 percent year on year in the second quarter. With AI-related exports and investment continuing to surge, Taiwan is on course for potentially double-digit economic growth this year. Yet promising prospects for economic growth have not translated into a comparable improvement in consumer sentiment. Taiwan's widely followed consumer confidence index stood at 65.01 in August, remaining well below 100, the threshold separating optimism from pessimism. The report also highlighted the deep integration of industrial chains on both sides of the Taiwan Strait and the importance of the mainland market, calling on Taiwan authorities to support healthy and orderly cross-Strait exchanges and help Taiwan businesses better share in the opportunities arising from the mainland's development. item.title: Mainland criticizes Taiwan's 'defense' spending, warns of resource depletion
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-28
Mainland criticizes Taiwan's 'defense' spending, warns of resource depletion Taiwan's Democratic Progressive Party authorities' squandering of public resources in pursuit of militarization will ultimately deplete the island, a Chinese defense ministry spokesperson said on Thursday. Commenting on the "defense" budget recently proposed by the Lai Ching-te authorities, Zhang Xiaogang, a spokesperson for the Ministry of National Defense, said the DPP authorities are acting against the mainstream aspirations of the Taiwanese public for peace and development. According to reports, the island's executive department has proposed a record NT$1.12 trillion ($35.2 billion) "defense" budget for 2027, exceeding NT$1 trillion for the first time. The figure represents an 18.2 percent increase from the 2026 budget. Zhang accused the Lai authorities of going to great lengths to curry favor with external forces, recklessly squandering public resources and pursuing militarization. "This has severely undermined the well-being of people on the island and will ultimately deplete Taiwan's resources, leaving the authorities facing their eventual downfall," Zhang said. He also stressed that the historical trend toward reunification is unstoppable, warning the DPP authorities that no matter how many military exercises they conduct, they cannot change the inevitable demise of "Taiwan independence".

item.title: Taiwan's DPP authorities pose biggest barrier to cross-Strait exchanges: spokeswoman
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-27
Taiwan's DPP authorities pose biggest barrier to cross-Strait exchanges: spokeswoman BEIJING -- Taiwan's Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) authorities have been acting as the biggest barrier to cross-Strait exchanges, a mainland spokeswoman said on Wednesday. Zhang Han, spokeswoman for the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office, made the remarks at a news conference when asked for comments on the DPP authorities' tight vetting on students applying for education exchange programs on the mainland. "The DPP authorities have gone extreme lengths to obstruct normal education and youth exchanges across the Strait," Zhang said, noting that the move has exposed their malicious agenda of escalating cross-Strait confrontation and antagonism. Peace, development, exchanges and cooperation represent mainstream public opinion in Taiwan, said Zhang. "The desire of compatriots across the Strait for closer ties and the momentum of exchanges and cooperation are unstoppable." While revealing that the DPP authorities are intentionally creating "information cocoon" in Taiwan, Zhang extended an invitation to the people of Taiwan to visit the mainland and see the real mainland for themselves. The spokeswoman also called on people from Taiwan to stay clear-headed in the face of Taiwan leader Lai Ching-te's separatist rhetoric and take a firm stand against "Taiwan independence" separatist acts.

item.title: Comment on Taiwan TV draws criticism on both sides of the Strait
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-27
Comment on Taiwan TV draws criticism on both sides of the Strait A comment made on a Taiwan TV program claiming that "there are no refrigerators in Beijing" has drawn criticism on both sides of the Taiwan Strait. "Such remarks, which are detached from reality, will only make a laughingstock of themselves," Zhang Han, a spokeswoman for the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office, said at a regular news conference on Wednesday. She said the Democratic Progressive Party authorities have imposed restrictions on and obstructed cross-Strait exchanges and interactions, deliberately creating an "information cocoon" on the island in an attempt to prevent Taiwan residents from learning about the mainland. "We welcome Taiwan residents to break through these barriers, visit the mainland more often and see for themselves the real and vibrant mainland," Zhang said. On a Taiwan TV program called Newswawawa, Liao Mei-ran, a self-described "fortune teller", claimed that during a visit to the mainland, she found "there were no refrigerators in Beijing, and people in Beijing did not have cold drinks". The remark drew attention on both sides of the Strait. Some Taiwan netizens said it reflected the extent to which the island has become an "information cocoon". "While it may appear that you are mocking the mainland, in fact, it is Taiwan that is embarrassing itself," one commenter wrote.

item.title: Ningbo-Taiwan Hockey Exchange Tournament Concludes in Fenghua, Ningbo, Forging Cross-Strait Friendships Through Sports
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-25
Ningbo-Taiwan Hockey Exchange Tournament Concludes in Fenghua, Ningbo, Forging Cross-Strait Friendships Through Sports Source: Taiwan.cnUpdated: 2026-08-25
Aug 25(Taiwan.cn)—On the morning of August 21, the "Tides Rise Across the Strait! Joy at Xuedou Mountain" Ningbo-Taiwan Hockey Exchange Tournament in Fenghua, Ningbo, drew to a rousing close. Nearly 40 athletes from Taiwan and Fenghua competed together, engaging in a cross-Strait sports dialogue with hockey as the medium. The competition venue buzzed with excitement. Players from both sides swung their sticks, passed rapidly, and demonstrated excellent teamwork and competitive spirit amid swift offensive-defensive transitions. "The atmosphere here is fantastic. Players from both sides respect one another and give their all on the pitch. The Fenghua athletes have made remarkable progress," said Mr. Zhuang, a player from the Taiwan team. He noted that hockey has a development history of nearly 50 years in Taiwan, with solid foundations there, while the sport has only gained popularity in Fenghua in recent years. "Still, we can feel their enthusiasm for learning and their rapid improvement. We hope that events like this will enable players from both sides to grow together through competition." "Sports are a vital bond for enhancing affection among cross-Strait compatriots. Going forward, we will continue to build more diverse exchange platforms. Focusing on sports, culture, tourism, talent, and other sectors, we will deepen practical cooperation between Fenghua and Taiwan, so that compatriots across the Strait grow closer through interaction," said an official from the Taiwan Affairs Office of Fenghua District.(Jointly reported by Taiwan.cn and the Taiwan Affairs Office of Fenghua, Ningbo City) Related Stories

item.title: Tanghe County Hosts Intangible Cultural Heritage Experience for Taiwan Compatriots and Relatives
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-25
Tanghe County Hosts Intangible Cultural Heritage Experience for Taiwan Compatriots and Relatives Source: Taiwan.cnUpdated: 2026-08-25
Aug 25(Taiwan.cn)—To promote China’s fine traditional culture, enrich the cultural lives of local Taiwan compatriots and their relatives, deepen cross-Strait cultural integration, and foster shared identity, the Taiwan Affairs Office of Tanghe County, Nanyang City, hosted a hands-on experience event featuring Song-style brocade round fans on August 19. Using intangible cultural heritage as an emotional bond, the event helped further bridge the psychological distance between compatriots across the Strait. At the venue, staff provided a detailed introduction to the cultural significance of Song brocade and the auspicious meanings associated with round fans. With pre-prepared materials-including brocade fabric, fan ribs, and tassels-they demonstrated the entire production process step by step. Participants received hands-on guidance on fabric bonding, accessory assembly, and fan-surface finishing, while their questions during the process were answered in detail. The Taiwan compatriots and their relatives focused intently on their creations and exchanged ideas with one another. By carefully cutting fabric, applying adhesives, and decorating with tassels, each participant completed their own unique intangible-heritage round fan. Through this immersive experience, attendees gained a firsthand appreciation for the charm of traditional intangible cultural crafts and developed a deeper understanding of the shared cultural roots that unite compatriots across the Strait.(Jointly reported by Taiwan.cn and the Taiwan Affairs Office of Tanghe County, Nanyang City) Related Stories

item.title: Taiwan's DPP authorities slammed for obstructing cross-Strait exchanges
item.description:
Published: 2026-02-11
Taiwan's DPP authorities slammed for obstructing cross-Strait exchanges BEIJING, Feb. 11 (Xinhua) -- A Chinese mainland spokesperson has condemned Taiwan's Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) authorities for imposing restrictions and obstacles on cross-Strait exchanges in pursuit of their "Taiwan independence" agenda and selfish gains. The DPP authorities, led by Lai Ching-te, are the biggest obstacle to cross-Strait interactions and their acts have drawn strong criticism from various sectors in Taiwan, Zhu Fenglian, a spokesperson for the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office, said at a regular press briefing on Wednesday. Zhu expressed the hope that Taiwan compatriots will firmly oppose the retrogressive actions of the DPP authorities and promote exchanges and cooperation across the Taiwan Strait in various fields. She noted that cross-Strait flight routes have been disrupted due to interference from the DPP authorities, with previously operated destinations yet to resume normal operations. In 2025, the average passenger load factor on cross-Strait routes reached 80 percent, reflecting the strong need for direct flights between the two sides of the Strait, Zhu said. "We hope that the Taiwan side will heed public opinion and lift unreasonable restrictions on cross-Strait air transport as soon as possible," she added.
